newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Asia's power-hungry economies need private capital.
newsitem.headline: Asia's power-hungry economies need private capital.

text.p: Asia requires US$100 billion a year in capital to develop new power generation plants, the majority of which would have to be raised from the private sector, according to the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
The ADB said booming Asian economies still faced a severe power shortage and planned to significantly boost coal-powered and hydrocarbon generation plants by the year 2000.

"The capital requirements of these generating capacity additions, as well as the associated transmission and distribution system expansion, are staggering," said Vladimir Bohun, deputy director of ADB's energy and financial sector.
"Together with the capital requirements in the hydrocarbon sector, they are estimated to exceed US$100 billion per annum," Bohun told an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) coal conference here.
Bohun said total power capacity in developing Asian nations more than doubled in the 1980s to 310 gigawatts (GW) in 1990, then rose to 408 GW in 1994, with 56 percent of it coal-fired.
China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Thailand, Hong Kong, Singapore, Korea and Taiwan all plan to boost capacity to about 640 GW by year 2000, he said.
But Bohun said only five to 10 percent of the necessary capital would be met by multilateral development banks.
He said the balance would have to come in the form of bilateral aid, export credits, commercial loans, internal cash generation of public utilities, direct private investments and domestic savings.

The ADB strongly encourages co-financing, said Bohun, adding that at the end of 1995, co-financiers had contributed US$21.9 billion to ADB-assisted projects, with official multilateral and bilateral sources contributing 69 percent of the funds.
But even with official aid, credits and private investment, capital requirements would not be met unless public utilities increased internal cash generation by raising charges, he said.
Current average electricity tariffs in Asia's developing nations ranged from four U.S. cents per kilowatt hour in India to 12 U.S. cents in the Philippines.
"In many (developing Asian nations) significant tariff increases will be unavoidable in the future," Bohun said.

Ted Atwood, international programmes manager of the U.S. Department of Energy, said world-wide power investment requirements between 1995 and 2010 were US$2.3 trillion, with US$1.5 trillion of this in developing and transitional nations.
But he said investment targets were reachable, with power taking only eight percent of total private investment and with US$20 trillion globally under professional funds management.

Bohun said coal, currently the source for about 54 percent of primary commercial energy supply in developing Asian nations, would continue to play a dominant role in the region's expanding power industry.
Over the next 15 years, its use worldwide was expected to grow at more than two percent a year, with growth in Asia expected to be three times stronger than in the developed world.

China and India would account for almost 60 percent of the global increase in coal demand by 2010, with China expected to use about 2.1 billion tonnes of coal a year and India about 500 million tonnes.
John Paffenbarger, an electricity market specialist with the International Energy Agency, said pollution controls added 20-25 percent to the cost of producing electricity.
But Bohun said the ADB was only willing to finance coal-fired power plants in Asia if they complied with environmental standards.
